prompt: Write an essay arguing whether students should be allowed to retake exams until they pass.
text:
# Should Students Be Allowed to Retake Exams Until They Pass?

Students should be allowed to retake exams until they pass, with some sensible limits. The purpose of school is to teach students something, and an exam is meant to measure whether that happened. If a student fails the first time but later masters the material, the second result describes what they know better than the first one did.

## Exams should measure learning, not timing

A single exam is a snapshot. A student may fail because of a sleepless night, a family crisis, or a slow start in a course that later clicked. Counting that one bad day as permanent punishes the student for the timing of their learning rather than the amount of it. A grade should tell an employer, a university, or a teacher what the student can do. If the student can now do it, the record should say so.

Many fields already work this way. Drivers can retake a road test. Aspiring lawyers, nurses, and electricians can retake licensing exams. Nobody argues that a driver who passed on the third attempt is unsafe on the road. What matters is that they can now drive well.

## Retakes encourage the right kind of effort

After failing, a student has two choices: give up or study what went wrong. Without a retake, giving up is the sensible choice, because the grade can't be repaired. With one, the student has a reason to go back, find the gaps, and fix them. That review is often where the deepest learning happens. Research on feedback supports this idea: people learn most when they can act on their mistakes soon after making them.

Retakes also reduce the kind of anxiety that harms performance. When one test carries all the weight, fear can crowd out thinking. Knowing that a failure is not final lets students approach the material with a clearer head.

## The objections

Critics raise three main concerns, and each has an answer.

**Students will not prepare for the first attempt.** This is possible, but it can be managed. Schools can require proof of study before a retake, such as completed practice work or a meeting with the teacher. They can also cap the highest grade on a retake, or use different questions each time. These rules keep the first attempt meaningful without closing the door.

**It is unfair to students who passed the first time.** Fairness depends on what the grade means. If the grade certifies knowledge, then a student who learned the material late has earned the same certification. The first-attempt students lose nothing, since their knowledge is just as real. Fairness would be hurt only if the retake were easier, which careful design can prevent.

**It costs teachers time.** This is the strongest objection. Writing, giving, and grading extra exams is real work. Schools can ease the burden with question banks, computer-graded tests, and scheduled retake sessions. If the cost still seems high, it is worth comparing with the cost of passing students on who never learned the material, or of having them repeat an entire course.

## Why "until they pass" still needs limits

Unlimited retakes with no conditions would invite gaming, such as sitting the exam just to see the questions. A good policy keeps the principle while adding guardrails: a waiting period between attempts, required remedial work, and fresh versions of the test. A student who cannot pass after several well-supported attempts also needs something other than another attempt, such as tutoring or a different learning plan. Repeating the same test is not a cure for a deeper problem.

## Conclusion

An exam is a tool for finding out what a student knows, and the goal of teaching is for students to know it. When a student fails and then learns the material, the system should recognize that success rather than freeze the earlier failure. Retakes, backed by reasonable limits and real support, make grades more accurate, give students a reason to keep trying, and keep the focus on learning. Schools should allow them.
